subject: Routing semantics for Dedicated Burst: fallback vs deny (customer-visible behavior)

From: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwoodinference.com>
To: Ravi Menon <ravi.menon@redwoodinference.com>, Elena Popov <elena.popov@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Ethan Park <ethan.park@redwoodinference.com>, Jordan Lee <jordan.lee@redwoodinference.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>, Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwoodinference.com>, Peter Holtz <peter.holtz@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Fri, Jun 20, 2025 at 9:14 AM PT
Subject: Routing semantics for Dedicated Burst: fallback vs deny (customer-visible behavior)

Team,

We need to lock routing semantics for the Dedicated “burst capacity” beta so that:
1) it’s deterministic/predictable (customer expectation + SRE runbooks)
2) it matches ADR-0142 (strict admission + cooldown; avoid preemption v1)
3) we don’t accidentally mask “burst denied” as generic overload

Proposed request path (Dedicated tenant with burst enabled):
A) Attempt baseline dedicated pool (tenant’s reserved capacity)
B) If baseline cannot accept (saturated/queue cap), attempt burst admission for eligible pool (policy)
C) If burst admission is denied OR burst pool saturated, decide between:
   - fallback (region/model variant), or
   - hard deny to customer

Open question: When do we permit fallback (C) vs force deny?

My current leaning:
- If burst is denied due to tenant-configured limit/policy (max_concurrency/max_tps/cooldown), we should NOT silently fall back to a different model or region. That would violate the customer’s guardrails and make billing attribution confusing.
- If burst is unavailable due to platform constraints (pool down / pool saturated / global circuit breaker), we can fallback only if customer explicitly enabled fallback in their Dedicated routing policy.

We need to land this for ENG-4824 and ensure docs match. Can folks reply with:
- what deny reason codes we want to expose (safe)
- how this maps to HTTP status (429 vs 503)
- what the default should be for beta tenants (fallback off?)

Mina

—

From: Ravi Menon <ravi.menon@redwoodinference.com>
To: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Elena Popov <elena.popov@redwoodinference.com>, Ethan Park <ethan.park@redwoodinference.com>, Jordan Lee <jordan.lee@redwoodinference.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>, Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwoodinference.com>, Peter Holtz <peter.holtz@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Fri, Jun 20, 2025 at 10:02 AM PT
Subject: Re: Routing semantics for Dedicated Burst: fallback vs deny (customer-visible behavior)

Agree with your leaning.

Key principle: “fallback” is a customer experience feature and should be opt-in per tenant. If they bought Dedicated for determinism + isolation, silent fallback (esp region) is a footgun.

I’d suggest we classify into two buckets:
1) POLICY_DENY (tenant-scoped, deterministic): exceed configured TPS/concurrency, cooldown active, burst disabled for tenant/region -> return 429.
2) PLATFORM_DENY (platform-scoped, transient): pool saturated, global circuit breaker open, pool unhealthy -> return 503.

Then fallback decision:
- If tenant routing policy allows fallback_on_platform_deny=true, we can attempt fallback only for PLATFORM_DENY.
- Never fallback on POLICY_DENY.

We should ensure the routing layer doesn’t “retry” burst multiple times in the same request chain. One admission attempt per request (else we create self-amplifying load).

Ravi

—

From: Jordan Lee <jordan.lee@redwoodinference.com>
To: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwoodinference.com>, Ravi Menon <ravi.menon@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Elena Popov <elena.popov@redwoodinference.com>, Ethan Park <ethan.park@redwoodinference.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>, Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwoodinference.com>, Peter Holtz <peter.holtz@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Fri, Jun 20, 2025 at 10:36 AM PT
Subject: Re: Routing semantics for Dedicated Burst: fallback vs deny (customer-visible behavior)

From policy engine side (ENG-4823), we can produce a deterministic decision object with:
- eligible: true/false
- deny_reason: one of a fixed enum
- retry_after_ms: optional (for cooldown)

Enums we’re planning (draft):
- BURST_DISABLED
- TENANT_NOT_ELIGIBLE_FOR_POOL
- LIMIT_EXCEEDED_TPS
- LIMIT_EXCEEDED_CONCURRENCY
- COOLDOWN_ACTIVE
- CIRCUIT_BREAKER_OPEN
- POOL_SATURATED
- POOL_UNHEALTHY

We can tag which are “tenant policy” vs “platform.” In the policy service we already know which are configuration-derived (limits/cooldown/eligibility) vs capacity gates (saturation/unhealthy/circuit breaker).

Question for routing: do you want policy service to decide fallback_allowed (boolean) based on tenant’s routing policy config, or do you want routing to handle that?

Also: if we return 429 for LIMIT_EXCEEDED + COOLDOWN_ACTIVE, should we always include Retry-After? (We can compute based on cooldown end timestamp.)

Jordan

—

From: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwoodinference.com>
To: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwoodinference.com>, Ravi Menon <ravi.menon@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Elena Popov <elena.popov@redwoodinference.com>, Ethan Park <ethan.park@redwoodinference.com>, Jordan Lee <jordan.lee@redwoodinference.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>, Peter Holtz <peter.holtz@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Fri, Jun 20, 2025 at 11:18 AM PT
Subject: Re: Routing semantics for Dedicated Burst: fallback vs deny (customer-visible behavior)

SRE POV:

1) Please don’t make fallback the default during beta. The fastest way to create a confusing incident is: customer sees quality change or data residency concern while we’re debugging a burst pool saturation event.

2) 429 vs 503 split is good, but we need to be careful about retries:
- 429 tends to trigger aggressive client retries if folks aren’t disciplined.
- 503 tends to trigger exponential backoff (usually), but sometimes upstream gateways retry too.

I’d like:
- For COOLDOWN_ACTIVE and LIMIT_EXCEEDED_* -> 429 + Retry-After header (seconds). Strongly word docs: “retry after this window or you will self-throttle.”
- For CIRCUIT_BREAKER_OPEN / POOL_SATURATED / POOL_UNHEALTHY -> 503 and include an internal-only reason code in logs/traces; customer-facing can be a coarse “burst temporarily unavailable.”

Also: we should include a request/trace annotation so oncall can answer “was this rejected because you hit your own limit, or because the pool was hot?” quickly.

Sean

—

From: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>
To: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Ravi Menon <ravi.menon@redwoodinference.com>, Elena Popov <elena.popov@redwoodinference.com>, Ethan Park <ethan.park@redwoodinference.com>, Jordan Lee <jordan.lee@redwoodinference.com>, Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwoodinference.com>, Peter Holtz <peter.holtz@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Fri, Jun 20, 2025 at 12:07 PM PT
Subject: Re: Routing semantics for Dedicated Burst: fallback vs deny (customer-visible behavior)

+1 to “fallback not default.” Product expectation for beta:
- We sell burst as controlled extra headroom, not as “we’ll route you somewhere else when things get busy.”

What we need customer-visible:
- Clear error semantics + guidance (when to retry, what knobs they can adjust)
- Clear statement that if burst denied due to their guardrail, we do not reroute.

For docs/PRD, can we standardize these headers?
- X-Redwood-Burst-Decision: admitted | denied | not_requested
- X-Redwood-Burst-Deny-Reason: (coarse set)

I’m fine if the deny reason is coarse to avoid giving away fleet details.

Can Mina/Ravi confirm the copy-level statements for:
- “burst admission is best-effort and may be unavailable during regional saturation events”
- “no preemption guarantee in v1; strict admission control”

Lauren

—

From: Ethan Park <ethan.park@redwoodinference.com>
To: Jordan Lee <jordan.lee@redwoodinference.com>, Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Ravi Menon <ravi.menon@redwoodinference.com>, Elena Popov <elena.popov@redwoodinference.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>, Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwoodinference.com>, Peter Holtz <peter.holtz@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Fri, Jun 20, 2025 at 1:23 PM PT
Subject: Re: Routing semantics for Dedicated Burst: fallback vs deny (customer-visible behavior)

Re Jordan question: I’d prefer policy service returns a stable “classification” + deny enum, and routing makes the final call based on tenant routing policy.

Reason: routing owns the full decision tree (baseline attempt result, model availability, region options). Policy service shouldn’t need to know about model fallbacks.

So policy response fields proposal:
- burst_allowed: bool
- deny_reason: enum
- deny_class: TENANT_POLICY | PLATFORM_CAPACITY
- retry_after_s: optional

Then routing:
- if deny_class=TENANT_POLICY -> return 429 (no fallback)
- if deny_class=PLATFORM_CAPACITY -> default return 503; if tenant config enables fallback_on_platform_deny -> attempt fallback chain

Also, we should pin “one policy evaluation per request” and cache policy result in-request context to avoid the retry-context bug class.

Ethan

—

From: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwoodinference.com>
To: Ravi Menon <ravi.menon@redwoodinference.com>, Elena Popov <elena.popov@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Ethan Park <ethan.park@redwoodinference.com>, Jordan Lee <jordan.lee@redwoodinference.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>, Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwoodinference.com>, Peter Holtz <peter.holtz@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Fri, Jun 20, 2025 at 3:47 PM PT
Subject: Re: Routing semantics for Dedicated Burst: fallback vs deny (customer-visible behavior)

Thanks all — summarizing decisions so we can implement + document (ENG-4824, and PRD update):

1) Default behavior (beta): NO fallback when baseline saturated + burst denied/unavailable.
   - Fallback is an explicit tenant routing policy flag; not enabled by default.

2) Deny classification:
   - TENANT_POLICY (burst guardrail / cooldown / ineligible): return 429.
   - PLATFORM_CAPACITY (pool saturation/unhealthy/circuit breaker): return 503.

3) Fallback rules:
   - Never fallback on TENANT_POLICY denies.
   - Optional fallback on PLATFORM_CAPACITY denies only if tenant config enables fallback_on_platform_deny=true.

4) Retry guidance:
   - For 429 due to cooldown/limits: include Retry-After (seconds) when available.
   - For 503: no Retry-After initially (keep it simple); docs will recommend exponential backoff.

5) Customer-visible signals (subject to docs review):
   - X-Redwood-Burst-Decision: admitted | denied | not_requested
   - X-Redwood-Burst-Deny-Class: tenant_policy | platform_capacity
   - X-Redwood-Burst-Deny-Reason: coarse enum (we’ll map internal reasons to a small public set)

6) Implementation notes:
   - Single burst admission attempt per request.
   - Cache policy result in-request context to avoid multi-eval / retry-context anomalies.

Action items:
- Mina/Ravi: add these semantics to ENG-4824 description + link ADR-0142.
- Jordan/Ethan: confirm deny enums + public mapping; add Retry-After computation for COOLDOWN_ACTIVE.
- Lauren: I’ll send you a short paragraph for PRD/docs copy on “best-effort, strict admission; no preemption in v1.”

Mina
